items.title: The Brandt Line is now badly outdated
items.claim: Why is the Brandt Line increasingly criticised?

options.text: It is an active political boundary
Drawn for the 1980 Brandt Commission report, it placed South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, UAE and Saudi Arabia in the 'poor South' — categories that 40 years of development have rendered misleading

items.reveal:
The Brandt Commission's 'North-South: A Programme for Survival' (1980), led by former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt, drew a line dipping south to include Australia and New Zealand in the 'rich North'.

Since 1980: South Korea's GDP per capita has risen from around $1,700 to over $34,000; China's from $300 to $12,500; the Gulf states have grown dramatically. Meanwhile parts of southern and eastern Europe have stagnated.

Alternatives: World Bank country income classifications (low/lower-middle/upper-middle/high), the UN's Least Developed Country (LDC) list, the BRICS+ grouping, and the political-solidarity concept of the 'Global South' (distinct from the geographical Brandt Line).
items.why: Categories age. Using a 1980 division to describe the 2020s misses four decades of differential development. Geography teachers using Brandt without context perpetuate outdated assumptions.

items.title: An aftershock larger than the mainshock becomes the new mainshock
items.claim: What is the relationship between mainshocks and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always at least one magnitude smaller

If a later quake in the sequence is larger, it is retrospectively called the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest; aftershocks typically follow Båth's law (around 1.2 magnitudes smaller) and Omori's law (rate decays as 1/t)
Aftershocks are unrelated to the mainshock

items.reveal:
Båth's law (1965) gives the largest aftershock as typically about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) describes the rate decay: aftershocks fall off as 1/t after the main event.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (M6.3, 22 February 2011) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (M7.1). Because it was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower, closer to the city centre, and hit during business hours.

Aftershock sequences can continue for years after large events — the New Madrid 1811-12 sequence still produces detectable aftershocks two centuries later.
items.why: Statistical naming hides hazard. A 'smaller' aftershock can do more damage than its mainshock if its location and depth are worse — Christchurch is the canonical case.

items.title: The Sahara was a green savannah 6,000 years ago
items.claim: Around 6,000 years ago, what is now the world's largest hot desert was something quite different. What was it?

options.text: It was already a desert; the Sahara has been arid for over 100,000 years
It was a savannah and grassland with lakes, rivers and human settlement — the 'African Humid Period'
It was a tropical rainforest like the Amazon today
It was covered by a shallow sea connected to the Mediterranean

items.reveal:
The African Humid Period lasted roughly 14,500 to 5,000 years ago. Cave paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show people herding cattle, swimming, and hunting hippos.

The cause was an orbital wobble — a stronger summer monsoon driven by changes in Earth's tilt and precession (Milankovitch cycles). When the monsoon retreated, the region desertified rapidly. Lake Chad was once larger than the Caspian Sea ('Lake Megachad').
items.why: Climate zones feel permanent on a human timescale. They are not. The Sahara's transformation in a few millennia is a reminder that 'natural' is just a snapshot of an unstable system.
